The nickel superalloy studied, referred to as Alloy 11, has a trimodal distribution of γ' precipitates: primary (429.99 nm), secondary (76.44 nm), and tertiary (25.32 nm).
In-situ STEM-EELS analysis was performed on thin TEM lamella samples during heating from room temperature to 950°C.
The dissolution of tertiary γ' precipitates was observed to initiate at lower temperatures (around 800°C) compared to secondary γ' precipitates (around 900°C).
The authors explained the difference in dissolution behavior using the Gibbs-Thomson effect, which predicts a higher interfacial concentration for smaller particles.
The reversed-growth approximation was used to show that the higher supersaturation parameter for the smaller tertiary γ' precipitates leads to faster dissolution kinetics.
The thermodynamic driving force for dissolution increases linearly with the degree of overheating above the solvus temperature, contributing to the earlier dissolution of smaller precipitates.
The EELS quantification approach used model-based methods to account for plural scattering effects and focus the analysis on regions with uniform sample thickness.
The in-situ STEM-EELS technique provided direct observation and quantification of the compositional changes in the different γ' precipitate populations during heating.
The findings have important implications for selecting appropriate heat treatment schedules to control the microstructural evolution and properties of nickel-based superalloys.
The authors noted that the diffusional phenomena observed in the thin TEM samples may appear accelerated compared to bulk behavior due to the reduced diffusion paths.
The authors highlighted the challenge of accurately quantifying the composition of the smallest tertiary γ' precipitates due to the surrounding matrix.
Simultaneous EELS analysis enabled the authors to map the elemental distributions of Ni, Co, Cr, Al, and Ti at the nanometer scale during in-situ heating.
The authors compared their findings to previous studies on the dissolution and reprecipitation of γ' particles in other nickel-based superalloys.
The authors emphasized the advantages of in-situ STEM-EELS over techniques like thermal analysis and neutron diffraction for studying the microstructural evolution of γ'-strengthened alloys.
